title: Beyond Appropriate Use of a Chatbot
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard opens with Krishiv Thakuria, a 17-year-old who co-taught two generative AI courses at MIT, to anchor his argument that most school AI literacy curricula are stuck teaching a 2023-era typing tutorial while the actual environment has moved on. He organizes real AI literacy into three tiers: Tier 1 is the tool frame (how models work, grounding, agents, using AI as a collaborator, evaluating both AI and human claims), Tier 2 is the influence frame (AI coming to you, notification-economy escalation, emotional bonds, companies' business models), and Tier 3 is the existential frame (apparent consciousness, agency instead of compliance, credentials becoming table stakes, broad preparation, AI as environment rather than tool). His core provocation is that almost every school effort lives in Tier 1, a thoughtful few reach Tier 2, and almost none touch Tier 3, yet Tier 3 is where students are actually forming identities, relationships, and career decisions. The ethics reframe he offers teachers is especially operational: stop pitching "don't cheat" as compliance, start pitching "own your future or outsource it" as agency, because compliance collapses the moment the surrounding commercial ecosystem makes compliance irrational. The final line is the summary: "The AI literacy nobody's teaching is the AI literacy everybody needs."
points: A three-tier model: Tool (how AI works, how to use it, how to evaluate it), Influence (push notifications, emotional attachment, business models), Existential (consciousness questions, agency framing, credentials-vs-capability, AI as environment).

The era of typing questions into a textbot is already ending as agentic AI that sets goals, plans, and executes multi-step tasks becomes standard, so students framed for the chatbot era are preparing for a world that is disappearing.
AI is one of the most powerful tools ever built for evaluating other people's claims, so teaching "use AI to be skeptical of everything" matters more than teaching "be skeptical of AI."

The agency reframe beats the integrity reframe in classrooms: "Do you want to own your future, or do you want to outsource it?" works where "don't cheat" collapses against the commercial ecosystem built around cheating.

Credentials are becoming table stakes rather than differentiators, so the future rewards people who can demonstrably do things, which argues for broad humanistic preparation alongside technical skill.
quotes: Most AI literacy curricula begin and end with the same lesson: here's how to use ChatGPT responsibly. Learn to prompt. Check your sources. Don't plagiarize. That's not AI literacy. That's a typing tutorial for 2023.

Students who think of AI as a thing they type questions into are preparing for a world that's already disappearing. The AI systems they'll encounter in college and careers will be coworkers, not chatbots, autonomous actors that take initiative, make decisions, and produce work product with minimal human oversight.

AI literacy shouldn't just mean "be skeptical of AI", it should mean "use AI to be skeptical of everything." In an information environment that's only getting noisier, messier, and more manipulative, teaching students to deploy AI as a critical thinking partner, a bullshit detector they carry in their pocket, might be the single most practically valuable thing we can do.

Here's the uncomfortable truth about AI ethics in education: telling students "don't cheat" doesn't work. Not because students are immoral, but because the framing is wrong. Students want the grade. They want the credential. They want the future opportunities those things unlock. "Academic integrity" is a compliance frame, and compliance frames collapse when the entire commercial ecosystem is designed to make compliance irrational from the student's perspective.

Every time you let AI do your thinking, you're not cheating the institution, you're cheating yourself out of the cognitive development that actually makes you capable. You can't build a school culture of integrity from 8 to 3 and then send students home into an ecosystem engineered to erode their agency.
